title: Relationships Between Tables
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of relationships between tables.
Apply one-to-one relationships in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn relationships between tables through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Relationships Between Tables matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: Relationships Between Tables
content_blocks.alt_text: One-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationship patterns are compared, with a junction table resolving many-to-many links.
content_blocks.caption: Choose relationship structure from the number of records that may match on each side.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Use relationships between tables to connect business meaning to table structure. A reliable relational design states what one row represents, how records are identified, and how related facts are connected without accidental duplication.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: One-to-one relationships, One-to-many relationships, Many-to-many relationships, Junction tables. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: One-to-one relationships
items.text: One-to-one relationships is a modeling choice. Identify the facts, decide which table owns each fact, then use keys and relationship tables to reduce duplication while preserving the business meaning.

items.title: Self-referencing relationships
items.text: Self-referencing relationships helps you learn how rows, columns, keys, relationships, schemas, and normalization work together to represent real-world facts without avoidable duplication. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT employee_id, full_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 80000
ORDER BY salary;
content_blocks.expected_output: BETWEEN includes both endpoints. Use timestamp half-open intervals when inclusive upper bounds could miss fractional seconds.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable local PostgreSQL database such as codeleaf_sql_lab after loading datasets/postgresql-lab-setup.sql. Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

content.task: Try it yourself: demonstrate relationships between tables using the sample schema. State what each returned row represents, test one edge case related to the lesson, and record the result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic one-to-one relationships and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
